title: Long-read metagenomics and methylation-based binning support the discovery of antibiotic resistance gene-host associations in complex communities.
data_url: Three open artefacts, all of which I opened. (1) Zenodo dataset 10.5281/zenodo.18239684, CC-BY-4.0, 88 FASTA files of assembled DNA fragments ('contigs') grouped into genome bins, 213,407,215 bytes total. (2) Zenodo software archive 10.5281/zenodo.21232712, GPL-3.0, one 3,885,973-byte zip of analysis scripts, mirrored at https://github.com/melinamarkkanen/Long-read-metagenomics-and-methylation-based-binning-support-the-discovery-of-ARG-host-associations. (3) ENA (European Nucleotide Archive) study PRJEB106782, 12 PacBio Sequel II sequencing runs, 13,922,997,736,338 submitted bytes (about 13.9 terabytes of raw BAM alignment files) - metadata only, nothing downloaded. The 492-column methylation feature table the authors actually trained on (merged_data.tsv) is in none of these.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC search on the DOI returned exactly 1 hit (PMID 42443941, first published 2026-07-13). It is NOT in PubMed Central: isOpenAccess 'N', inEPMC 'N', inPMC 'N', hasSuppl 'N', fullTextXML returns HTTP 404, supplementaryFiles returns HTTP 404, and the PMC identifier converter replies 'Identifier not found in PMC'. The only full-text link Europe PMC offers is the publisher DOI marked 'Subscription required'. Per my own project rules I did not scrape the publisher site, so I never saw the Data availability statement or any supplementary table. Everything below I found through repository application programming interfaces instead. I searched Zenodo and found both records for this work and listed them: record 18239684 is 88 FASTA files, CC-BY-4.0, which I downloaded in full (242 MB on disk, 213,407,215 bytes as listed) and parsed myself - 1,039 FASTA headers, 1,030 unique contig identifiers (9 appear in two files because the authors deposited both a filtered 'f' and an unfiltered version of some bins), 213,388,278 base pairs, smallest bin 515,604 bp, median 1,749,318 bp, largest 7,744,709 bp, spread over 59 distinct sample-cluster bins across 9 wastewater samples (EFF1 3 bins, EFF2 7, EFF3 5, INF1 8, INF2 11, INF3 12, SLU1 12, SLU2 16, SLU3 14). Record 21232712 is one 3,885,973-byte code zip which I downloaded and listed: 55 entries, identical to the GitHub tree (54 entries, API reports truncated=false). I read every README and both methylation-feature scripts. The ONE data table in the whole deposit is HAMBI_analyses/HAMBI_labels.txt, 990,296 bytes, which I parsed with Python's csv module: 1,990 data rows, 17 tab-separated columns (contig_id, d, p, c, o, f, g, s, element, str, All, and six pre-pasted 'Domain to X' strings), zero empty cells, 669 rows filled entirely with the literal string 'NA', leaving 1,321 rows with a real species label; 15 unique species and 15 unique strain codes; element types 1,051 chromosome, 72 chromosome_1, 51 chromosome_2 and 147 plasmid rows across six plasmid spellings; 5 sequencing barcodes with 305 to 713 contigs each. Largest species Citrobacter_B_koseri 254 contigs, smallest Kluyvera_intermedia 2. I also mined the 14,868,991-byte notebook UMAP_analysis_WW.ipynb: two saved Plotly figures embed real per-contig tables, which I extracted to CSV myself - sample INF3 with 9,778 unique contigs and sample SLU1 with 24,736, each carrying columns UMAP1, UMAP2, contig, mod_count (integer count of detected modified bases), ARG_name, ARG_count, contig_length (base pairs) and fARGene_class. Only 56 INF3 contigs and 34 SLU1 contigs have a non-empty ARG_name; 128 and 121 respectively have a non-empty fARGene_class. I then joined the deposited bins to these tables on contig identifier: all 167 INF3 binned contigs and all 118 SLU1 binned contigs are present in the tables (100% join), but they are only 1.71% and 0.48% of the contigs in those samples, and of the 56 and 34 resistance-gene-carrying contigs only 6 and 7 fall inside any deposited bin. I queried the ENA portal application programming interface for PRJEB106782 (found via NCBI BioProject search, accession PRJEB106782, submitter 'MMX-Group', registered 2026-02-10) and summed the bytes myself: 12 PacBio Sequel II runs, 13,922,997,736,338 submitted bytes (13.9 TB of BAM), 1,306,752,359,255 bytes of ENA-converted fastq. ENA lists zero 'analysis' objects and zero assemblies for this project, so no intermediate files there. I downloaded no sequencing data. I confirmed via the Zenodo creator search that these two records are the only deposits by this author for this work.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Essentially the whole paper. I have only the 269-word structured abstract from Europe PMC plus the 332-word abstract of the earlier preprint (Europe PMC PPR1268423, DOI 10.64898/2026.02.18.26346558, 2026-02-22), whose full text also 404s in Europe PMC. Unverified by me, because no file contains them: the claim that the approach was 'validated by a synthetic community with known bacterial composition' and whatever accuracy figure backs it; the identity of the 'several previously unreported ARGs and ARG-host linkages'; that Arcobacter carries a latent beta-lactamase gene and what 'high predicted mobility potential' means numerically; the blaMCA pdif-module findings; and the named hosts Simplicispira, Phycisphaerae and Bacteroidales. I never saw a single figure, a single supplementary table, the Methods, or the Data availability statement. Crucially I could not verify ANY taxonomic identity for the 59 deposited wastewater bins: the READMEs say CheckM2 (bin completeness) and GTDB-Tk (taxonomy) were run, but neither tool's output table is deposited, so the paper's central product - which bacterium hosts which resistance gene - exists for me only as prose in the abstract. I also did not run the authors' pipeline, did not recompute any position weight matrix, and did not download or inspect any PacBio file.

a1_downloadable.note: PASSES, and generously. No login, no access application, no dead link. I downloaded all 88 genome-bin FASTA files (213,407,215 bytes, CC-BY-4.0), the 3,885,973-byte code archive (GPL-3.0), and the full GitHub tree, and I listed the 12 raw sequencing runs in ENA study PRJEB106782 through its open application programming interface. The paper itself is the only thing I could not reach: it is not in PubMed Central, so there is no full text and no supplementary file list available through Europe PMC.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: PASSES for exactly one sub-task and fails for the paper's headline one. For the synthetic-community validation, the species label IS literally a column: HAMBI_labels.txt has columns 'd' through 's' (domain to species) and 'str' (strain code), with 1,321 of 1,990 rows filled - I counted them. For the wastewater result that the paper is actually about, the label (which bacterium hosts which resistance gene) is a column in nothing: the 59 deposited bins arrive as bare FASTA with no taxonomy file, so you would have to install and run GTDB-Tk against a 100+ GB reference database to build the label yourself.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAILS. This is the kill. The authors' own notebook Random_Forest_analysis_HAMBI.ipynb opens its training data with pd.read_csv('/scratch/project_2006608/Methylation/HAMBI_data/merged_data.tsv') - a 492-feature-column table of methylation position weight matrices (I read the construction recipe in HAMBI_analyses/README.md and the code in src/scoring_matrices_HAMBI.py: 41 positions from -20 to +20, times 4 nucleotides, times 3 modification types m4C, m6A and generic modified_base). That file is in neither Zenodo record, not in the GitHub tree (54 entries, API confirms not truncated), and ENA lists no analysis objects for PRJEB106782. The inputs are therefore a path on a Finnish supercomputer. Rebuilding them means pulling 13.9 TB of PacBio BAM from ENA, realigning per contig, running ipdSummary from PacBio SMRT Link to produce a basemods GFF per contig, then running the authors' matrix script - and my project rules forbid downloading raw sequencing data at all. The only features that ARE deposited are a 2-dimensional UMAP projection of those 492 columns, which I extracted for 2 of 9 samples; a projection fitted separately per sample with a fixed seed is not a reusable feature space.

a4_units_stated.note: PASSES on what exists, and the code makes it unambiguous. The feature values are dimensionless natural logarithms of an observed-over-expected nucleotide frequency ratio - I read the line 'PWM.at[nucleotide, pos] = np.log(normalized_count)' in src/scoring_matrices_HAMBI.py. In the per-contig tables I extracted, mod_count is an integer count of detected modified bases, contig_length is in base pairs, ARG_count is an integer, and UMAP1/UMAP2 are unitless embedding coordinates. The label columns are categorical names. Nothing is ambiguous about units here.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS for the real task, marginal for the toy one. Counts I made myself: 1,321 species-labelled contigs in HAMBI_labels.txt (above the ~400 classification floor, but with no features attached); 1,030 unique contigs in 59 deposited wastewater bins; and across the two samples whose per-contig tables I could recover, 90 resistance-gene-carrying contigs (56 in INF3, 34 in SLU1) of which only 13 sit inside a deposited bin. The paper's unit of interest is the resistance-gene-to-host link, and the deposited files support on the order of ten such links per sample. Also note the 1,321 labelled contigs come from a single 5-sample synthetic community of 15 species, so the effective number of independent groups is 15, not 1,321.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: What is deposited: 242 MB on disk (213,407,215 bytes of bin FASTA plus 15 MB of code, notebooks and the one label file) - entirely comfortable, and I processed all of it in under a minute. What the task needs: 13,922,997,736,338 bytes (about 13.9 terabytes) of PacBio Sequel II BAM in ENA study PRJEB106782, which I summed from the ENA application programming interface, plus per-contig realignment and a PacBio SMRT Link ipdSummary run for every one of roughly 35,000 contigs per sample.
a6_fits_laptop.note: FAILS for anything that needs the methylation features, which is the entire project. 13.9 TB is 2,800 times my 5 GB working-set ceiling, my rules forbid downloading raw sequencing data, and ipdSummary is a cluster tool that expects the original kinetics-tagged BAM. Passes trivially for the deposited subset, and that gap between 242 MB of deposited output and 13.9 TB of required input is exactly why this is a reject.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: FAILS because the comparison is impossible, not because I caught a contradiction. The paper is not in PubMed Central (hasSuppl 'N', fullTextXML 404), so there is no row count, table or figure to check the files against, and that unverifiability is itself the risk this check exists to catch. The one internal consistency check I could run passed cleanly: the top-level README lists reference genomes for 18 synthetic-community strains and marks 3 of them (HAMBI_0262 Brevundimonas bullata, HAMBI_2159 Trinickia caryophylli, HAMBI_2494 Paraburkholderia kururiensis) as 'not detected by BLASTn', and HAMBI_labels.txt contains exactly 15 species - 18 minus 3. One oddity worth flagging: the README calls the community '36 species' while only 18 have reference genomes, so half the community can never be labelled.

a8_label_provenance.note: PASSES for the synthetic-community label and FAILS for the paper's novel claim, which is the part that matters. The HAMBI species label traces to a physical measurement: a BLASTn best hit with at least 1,000 bp of alignment against reference genomes sequenced from pure isolates (NCBI BioProject PRJNA1047486, Hogle et al. 2024) - homology, not another model's prediction. Two caveats I read in the code. First, the README says the label file was 'modified further in excel', so a hand-edited step sits between the alignment and the label. Second, and more serious, the paper's novel 'latent' resistance genes are called by fARGene, a hidden Markov model - a model output - so the fARGene_class column I extracted (128 INF3 and 121 SLU1 contigs) cannot be used as ground truth, while the established-resistance-gene column comes from BLASTn against the ResFinder database at 90% identity with manual de-duplication ('Manually fix those contigs that have multiple'), i.e. computable from the contig sequence and therefore pure leakage if your features include that sequence. Separate leakage note nobody states: the 492 features are nucleotide frequencies in a 41-base window, so they partly encode plain local sequence composition - the very signal that conventional composition-based binners use - which means a feature-ablation control is mandatory before believing that 'methylation' is doing the work.

existing_models.name: mBin (Beaulaurier et al., Nature Biotechnology 2017/2018, 'Metagenomic binning and association of plasmids with bacterial host genomes using DNA methylation')
existing_models.score_and_split: I retrieved the record via Europe PMC (PMID 29227468, PMC5762413, DOI 10.1038/nbt.4037, 136 citations) and read the abstract. It is the direct ancestor of this paper: the same idea (PacBio single-molecule real-time sequencing detects bacterial DNA methylation; use those 'endogenous epigenetic barcodes' to bin reads and contigs to species and strain level, and to link plasmids to hosts), validated on synthetic and real microbiome data. I did not retrieve the paper body, so I verified no accuracy number and no split. The code is public at github.com/fanglab/mbin with documentation at mbin.readthedocs.io (titles seen in search results; I did not list the repository).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: From the abstract only: they position methylation binning as complementary to composition and abundance binning for cases where those 'cannot fully distinguish closely related species and strains'. I did not retrieve their discussion, so I cannot name the gap they flagged.

existing_models.name: Nanomotif (MicrobialDarkMatter group, bioRxiv preprint 10.1101/2024.04.29.591623, Europe PMC PPR846572)
existing_models.score_and_split: The closest competitor, and it is more advanced than this paper's pipeline on the machine-learning axis. I retrieved its abstract through Europe PMC: it identifies methylation motifs from Oxford Nanopore all-context methylation models and uses them for database-independent contamination removal from genome bins and for host association of plasmids. Its include_contigs module assigns unbinned contigs by training three classifiers (random forest, linear discriminant analysis, k-nearest neighbours) on each bin's methylation pattern - directly comparable to this paper's random forest. Search snippets report mean sensitivity 89% and precision 91% for contamination detection across 50 leave-one-contig-out datasets; I did NOT retrieve the preprint body, so treat both numbers as unverified. Code and documentation are public (github.com/MicrobialDarkMatter/nanomotif, nanomotif.readthedocs.io).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - I read only the abstract. The platform difference is the obvious open question: Nanomotif is built on Oxford Nanopore basecall models, this paper on PacBio kinetics, and nobody has shown the two produce interchangeable motif features.

existing_models.name: Methylation binning of the Sippewissett 'pink berry' consortium (Jaffe et al., ISME Journal 2022)
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved via Europe PMC (PMID 35459792, PMC9296519, DOI 10.1038/s41396-022-01242-7, 28 citations), abstract read. Uses strain-specific restriction-modification methylation profiles to bin long-read metagenomic contigs and reports the largest circularised genome then recovered from a metagenome (7.9 Mb, over 600 transposons), plus horizontal gene transfer detection between two symbionts. It is a demonstration on one community rather than a released classifier, so there is no held-out score. Open access with supplementary files, which makes it a plausible external validation set.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved beyond the abstract, which frames the problem as mechanisms of rapid genomic change confounding current genome-recovery approaches.

existing_models.name: The deep-learning composition-and-coverage binners this would have to beat: VAMB, SemiBin2, COMEBin, GraphMB, and the classical MetaBAT2
existing_models.score_and_split: Named from my background knowledge and from a retrieved review title ('Solving genomic puzzles: computational methods for metagenomic binning', PMC11289683, seen in search results but not opened). I verified no number for any of them here. They matter for scoring because they define the baseline a methylation binner must beat, and because they are open, widely benchmarked on standard challenges, and run on a laptop - which is the opposite of this paper's situation.

existing_models.name: This paper's own model: a scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier on 492 methylation position-weight-matrix features, plus UMAP for visualisation
existing_models.score_and_split: I read the notebook myself (notebooks/Random_Forest_analysis_HAMBI.ipynb, 38,190 bytes, 33 cells, GPL-3.0). It trains with a plain sklearn train_test_split at six taxonomic ranks (species, genus, family, order, class, phylum), with seed 98, and repeats the whole thing after filtering contigs to at least 50, 100, 200 and 500 detected modified bases. Three things make it not a usable baseline for me. Every output cell is empty, so no score is saved anywhere. The split is random over contigs, and contigs from the same genome are near-duplicates, so a random split leaks heavily - a leave-one-strain-out split is the honest one and was not used. And the input file lives at /scratch/project_2006608/..., so it cannot be run at all.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: From the abstract only: 'identification bottlenecks stem from the limitations of shotgun metagenomic sequencing and bioinformatic methods'. One self-reported choice in HAMBI_analyses/README.md is worth recording verbatim because it is a methodological flag: modification types with fewer than 50 detected sites 'are filled with 0 matrices which increased the models performance' - a preprocessing decision selected on model performance.

backbone.name: No backbone matches the data that is actually deposited. A DNA language model (DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer or HyenaDNA, all with open weights) would fit the 213 MB of contig sequence I downloaded, but it encodes sequence only - it has no notion of a methylated base - so freezing it and fitting a head would rebuild a composition-based binner, which is precisely the approach methylation binning exists to improve on. There is no pretrained model for bacterial methylation position weight matrices.
backbone.hardware: A frozen DNA language model over 213,388,278 base pairs of contig sequence, chunked into 512-base-pair windows, is roughly 420,000 forward passes - call it 10 to 15 hours on this 16 GB CPU laptop, done once and cached. That is affordable, but it answers a different question than the paper asks. The paper's own feature extraction (per-contig realignment plus PacBio ipdSummary over 13.9 TB) is cluster work, not laptop work.
backbone.licence: Clean throughout, which is the one unambiguously good thing here. Zenodo dataset CC-BY-4.0, code GPL-3.0 (so a derivative pipeline must also be GPL), ENA reads open. DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA weights are openly downloadable; Nucleotide Transformer is CC-BY-NC (non-commercial).

integration.partner_dataset: REBASE, the restriction enzyme and methyltransferase database, is the natural and specific partner: it maps methyltransferase genes to the exact DNA motifs they methylate. Secondary partners: GTDB release 220 via GTDB-Tk for bin taxonomy (the authors ran it but deposited no output), ResFinder and CARD for resistance-gene identity, and the companion study PRJEB83306 / Microbiology Spectrum 2025 (PMC12772301) for a second wastewater dataset from the same plant.
integration.join_key: The methylation motif string itself (for example GATC) joins to REBASE; a taxon name joins to GTDB; a resistance gene name such as sul4_1 or erm(F)_3 joins to ResFinder; and contig identifiers of the form s1.ctg000044l join the deposited bins to the per-contig tables I extracted - that join I actually tested and it was 100% (118 of 118 for SLU1, 167 of 167 for INF3).
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Can a bacterium's methylation motif repertoire be predicted from its methyltransferase gene content alone, so that a resistance gene found on a loose contig could be assigned to a host by matching its observed methylation pattern against motifs predicted from genomes, without needing a methylated reference of that host? That is a genuinely good question that neither this dataset nor REBASE answers alone - but it needs the per-contig motif calls, and those are the exact files not deposited, so the join has nothing to join on.

controls.positive_control: Two good ones exist in principle and one is already built in. The synthetic community is itself the control: 15 species whose reference genomes are public (NCBI BioProject PRJNA1047486), so a working classifier must separate them, and the authors used it exactly that way. Cheaper and sharper: the textbook Escherichia coli Dam and Dcm motifs (GATC and CCWGG) must appear in any Enterobacteriaceae contig's methylation profile - and the community contains Citrobacter, Kluyvera and Morganella. Neither is runnable by me, because both need the motif-level data.
controls.negative_control: Three, all cheap if the features existed, and the third is the one I would insist on. Shuffle the species labels across the 1,321 labelled contigs and confirm accuracy collapses to the per-species prior. Re-split by strain rather than at random (the authors used a plain random train_test_split over contigs from only 15 genomes, which leaks badly) and watch the number fall. And ablate the feature blocks: the 492 features are nucleotide frequencies in a 41-base window, so run the model on the generic 'modified_base' block alone versus the m4C and m6A blocks alone - if plain local sequence composition carries the signal, 'methylation-based binning' is a misnomer. I could not run any of these.
controls.external_validation: A real second source exists and is open: the same group's companion study on the sul4 resistance gene (Microbiology Spectrum 2025, PMC12772301, ENA PRJEB83306 - I listed its 18 runs, 229.3 GB of fastq from the same nine wastewater samples on both Illumina and PacBio), plus the ISME Journal 2022 pink-berry methylation dataset and Nanomotif's Oxford Nanopore benchmarks. The platform contrast (PacBio kinetics versus Nanopore basecall models) is the most interesting external test available. No publication-year or source column exists in any deposited file, so the cheap temporal split is not available.

honest_claim_h3: With only the deposited files, the strongest honest claim is: 'the authors grouped 1,030 wastewater contigs into 59 methylation-similarity bins, which is 0.5 to 1.7 percent of the contigs in each sample, and 13 of the roughly 90 contigs carrying a known resistance gene fall inside one of those bins' - and since no taxonomic identity is deposited for any bin, no statement about which bacterium hosts which resistance gene can be checked at all.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a DNA fragment's chemical-modification fingerprint to predict which bacterial species it came from, linking resistance genes to their hosts.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one assembled DNA fragment ('contig') from a mixed microbial sample, described by 492 numbers that summarise which DNA letters sit in the 20 bases either side of each chemically modified base, split by modification type. The label file I opened covers 1,990 contigs of which 1,321 carry a species name, but the 492 numbers themselves are deposited nowhere - I verified they live only on the authors' supercomputer.
plain_idea.predict: Which of 15 bacterial species the fragment belongs to. The true answer comes from aligning the fragment (with BLASTn, at least 1,000 matching bases) against reference genomes of the known strains that were mixed into the synthetic community, each sequenced separately from a pure culture - so it is a real measurement, not another model's guess.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Wastewater surveillance groups and antimicrobial-resistance epidemiologists want to know which bacteria are carrying newly emerging resistance genes; today that needs culturing, which usually fails for environmental bacteria. A method that reads the answer off one sequencing run would change what they can monitor, and even a failure would tell us whether methylation patterns carry species information beyond what plain DNA composition already gives.

ml_idea: Three framings, and all three die on the same fact: the authors deposited their conclusions and their code but not their features. (1) Reproduce or improve the species classifier. The feature table is a hard-coded path, /scratch/project_2006608/Methylation/HAMBI_data/merged_data.tsv, in the authors' own notebook; it is in neither Zenodo record and not in the 54-file GitHub tree. Regenerating it means 13.9 terabytes of PacBio BAM from ENA study PRJEB106782 (a number I summed from the ENA application programming interface), per-contig realignment, and a PacBio SMRT Link ipdSummary run per contig - forbidden by my rules and impossible on a laptop. (2) Predict resistance-gene presence from the deposited per-contig tables. I did recover these by mining the saved Plotly figures inside UMAP_analysis_WW.ipynb: 9,778 INF3 contigs and 24,736 SLU1 contigs with modification count, contig length and resistance-gene columns. But the label is computed from the contig sequence by BLASTn against ResFinder (leakage by construction), the two usable features are a per-sample UMAP projection that is not comparable across samples, there are only 90 positive contigs, and 7 of 9 samples were never plotted. (3) Train a DNA language model head on the 213 MB of deposited bin sequence. That rebuilds a composition-based binner and quietly abandons the paper's actual contribution. What IS salvageable is a short methods note rather than a project, built on four things I verified in the files and nobody has written down: the 59 deposited bins hold 1,030 contigs, which is 0.48% of sample SLU1 and 1.71% of sample INF3, so the method bins about one contig in a hundred; only 13 of roughly 90 resistance-gene-carrying contigs land in any bin, which bounds the yield of resistance-gene-to-host links at about ten per sample; the bins carry no taxonomy file even though the README says GTDB-Tk was run, so the paper's central claim is uncheckable from the deposit; and the 492 'methylation' features are nucleotide frequencies in a 41-base window, which partly re-encodes the local sequence composition that conventional binners already use - a feature-ablation control that the deposited notebook never runs. A one-line request to the authors for merged_data.tsv and the GTDB-Tk output would turn this from a reject into a genuinely interesting candidate.

effort.compute_note: Two sets of numbers and the gap between them is the verdict. For the deposited data, these are measured, not estimated: the 88-file 213,407,215-byte Zenodo download took a few minutes, parsing all 1,039 FASTA headers and 213.4 million base pairs took about 10 seconds, the 990,296-byte label file parsed instantly, and extracting the two embedded Plotly tables from the 14.9 MB notebook took under 5 seconds - so about 4 hours of real work to assemble everything openable into one table, peak memory around 1 GB. The random-forest baseline on 1,321 rows by 492 columns would finish in well under a minute, so cv_run_minutes is 1; needs_gpu is false because the baseline is scikit-learn. embedding_hours of 12 is an estimate, not a timing: roughly 420,000 512-base-pair windows covering the 213 Mbp of bin sequence, at about 10 windows per second for a small DNA language model on this CPU. None of it matters, because the paper's own features need 13.9 TB of PacBio BAM and a cluster-only PacBio tool.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open notebooks/Random_Forest_analysis_HAMBI.ipynb (38,190 bytes, free on GitHub), read cell 5, and note that it loads /scratch/project_2006608/Methylation/HAMBI_data/merged_data.tsv. Then search both Zenodo records and the GitHub tree for that filename. Five minutes, no download needed, and it ends the project: the 492-column methylation feature table the paper is built on is not deposited anywhere. Second-cheapest, ten more minutes: list ENA study PRJEB106782 and sum submitted_bytes (13,922,997,736,338) to confirm that regenerating it is off the table.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A at A3, with A5 and A6 failing behind it - all checked in the files, because no full text exists to be misled by. The kill is A3: the authors deposited the conclusions and the code but not the features. Their own notebook loads training data from /scratch/project_2006608/Methylation/HAMBI_data/merged_data.tsv, a 492-column table of methylation position weight matrices (41 positions times 4 nucleotides times 3 modification types, per the recipe in HAMBI_analyses/README.md and the np.log(q/p0) line in src/scoring_matrices_HAMBI.py), and that file is in neither Zenodo record, not in the GitHub tree (54 entries, API confirms not truncated), and not in ENA, which lists zero analysis objects for PRJEB106782. Rebuilding it means 13,922,997,736,338 bytes - 13.9 terabytes - of PacBio Sequel II BAM, which I summed myself from the ENA application programming interface, plus a PacBio SMRT Link ipdSummary run per contig; my rules forbid downloading raw sequencing data and 13.9 TB is 2,800 times my working-set ceiling (A6). A5 compounds it with numbers I counted: the entire deposited product is 88 FASTA files, 1,039 headers, 1,030 unique contigs, 213,388,278 base pairs, in 59 bins across 9 samples - and those bins carry no taxonomy file at all, even though the README says CheckM2 and GTDB-Tk were run, so the paper's headline claim about which bacteria host which resistance gene cannot be checked from the deposit in any form. I did find real data by mining the saved Plotly figures inside the 14.9 MB notebook (9,778 INF3 and 24,736 SLU1 contigs with modification counts, lengths and resistance-gene columns), and the join to the bins was perfect (118 of 118 and 167 of 167 on contig identifier), which produced the most useful numbers here: the bins cover only 0.48% and 1.71% of contigs in those two samples, and just 13 of roughly 90 resistance-gene-carrying contigs land in any bin. A2 passes only narrowly - the species label is a genuine column in HAMBI_labels.txt (1,321 of 1,990 rows filled, 15 species, zero empty cells, and it is internally consistent with the README's 18 reference strains minus 3 marked undetected) - and A8 passes for that label because it traces to BLASTn against isolate reference genomes rather than a model. But A8 fails for the paper's novel part: the 'latent' resistance genes come from fARGene, a hidden Markov model, so that column is a model's output, and the established-gene column is BLASTn against ResFinder with manual de-duplication, i.e. computable from the sequence. Three things are good and none rescue it: licences are clean (CC-BY-4.0 data, GPL-3.0 code, open ENA), the code is unusually well documented for a wet-lab group, and a real second dataset exists for external validation (the same group's sul4 study, PMC12772301, ENA PRJEB83306). Two file-level observations worth sending to the authors: the notebook's plain random train_test_split over contigs drawn from only 15 genomes leaks heavily and should be leave-one-strain-out, and the README states that modification types with under 50 sites were zero-filled because it 'increased the models performance', which is a preprocessing choice made on the test metric. One email asking for merged_data.tsv and the GTDB-Tk output would move this from reject to verify_first.
